w: Every day at noon, two mechanical goats above the clock butt heads for the crowds below - a party trick that has outlasted the government this building once housed. Raised in the 1550s over a 13th-century core, it ran the city until 1939. Now it holds a museum, and the goats still keep the schedule.
s: Mechanical goats have butted heads here since the 1550s
_facts: Originally built late 13th century following the medieval city's founding in 1253
Rebuilt 1550-1560 in Mannerist style by Giovanni Battista di Quadro, with an ornate loggia
Served as seat of local government until 1939; now houses a museum
Mechanical fighting goats appear above the clock daily at noon - a major tourist draw

w: Poznan's grandest Baroque church took half a century to build and somehow escaped the war that flattened so much else nearby. Polish and Italian masters raised Roman-style columns inside; the 17-metre altar came later, carved by Pompeo Ferrari. Benedict XVI made it a minor basilica in 2010 - Perpetual Help, indeed.
s: The finest Baroque church in Poland, spared by luck
_facts: Full name: Basilica of Our Lady of Perpetual Help, Saints Mary Magdalene and Stanislaus of Szczepanów
Built 1651-1701 by Polish and Italian masters in Baroque style with Corinthian columns
18th-century main altar, 17m tall, designed by Pompeo Ferrari
Spared destruction in WWII; raised to minor basilica by Benedict XVI in 2010

w: Kaiser Wilhelm II did not just commission this palace - he pushed his own suggestions into the design, and the result is a squat, fortress-like pile that looks older than 1910. It has housed German and Polish government offices in alternating waves ever since, through two world wars and every regime change between.
s: The Kaiser's own palace, still doing government work
_facts: Built 1910 by architect Franz Schwechten for Wilhelm II, German Emperor, with his own design input
Housed German government offices to 1918 and during WWII
Housed Polish government offices 1918-1939 and 1945-present

w: One of the ring of 19th-century forts built to defend Poznan became, within weeks of the 1939 invasion, one of the first Nazi death camps on Polish soil - Konzentrationslager Posen. Somewhere between 4,500 and 20,000 people, mostly local Poles, died here before the war's end. It stands today as a museum, and a warning.
s: A 19th-century fort became one of the first Nazi death camps
_facts: Officially Konzentrationslager Posen, set up in occupied Poznań during WWII
Located in one of the 19th-century forts ringing the city
Between 4,500 and 20,000 people died imprisoned there, mostly Poles from the region

w: An artificial lake borrows its name from the Knights of Malta, who held this land from 1187 - centuries before anyone dammed the Cybina River to flood it, in 1952. What emerged is now Poznan's playground: a rowing course that has hosted World Championships, an artificial ski slope, an ice rink, and a lakeside zoo.
s: Poznan's own lake, dammed into existence in 1952
_facts: Artificial lake formed 1952 by damming the Cybina River, 2.2km long
Name derives from the Knights Hospitaller (Knights of Malta), given the land in 1187
One of Europe's oldest man-made rowing venues; hosted Rowing World Cup and ICF Canoe Sprint World Championships
Recreational attractions on its banks include a ski slope, ice rink, zoo and narrow-gauge railway

w: Founded in 1249 under Duke Przemysl I, Poznan's Royal Castle spent most of the 20th century as a ruin - flattened in the Second World War and left that way for decades. What stands today is a partial reconstruction of one of Poland's oldest royal residences, rebuilt in fragments rather than restored whole.
s: A 1249 royal seat, rebuilt from ruins in fragments
_facts: Dates from 1249, founded during the reign of Przemysł I
Largely destroyed during the Second World War
Has since been partly rebuilt

w: Five centuries of Polish painting share the walls here with Italian, Spanish, Dutch and German canvases, alongside a numismatic collection and a gallery of applied arts - the kind of sprawling, encyclopedic museum that rewards an afternoon of aimless wandering rather than a highlights-reel dash through one wing.
s: Five centuries of Polish painting, plus the rest of Europe
_facts: State-owned, one of the largest museums in Poland
Houses Polish painting from the 16th century onward
Also holds Italian, Spanish, Dutch and German painting, numismatics and applied arts collections

w: Seven craters pock a patch of woodland on Poznan's northern edge - scars from a meteorite that broke apart and struck Earth here thousands of years ago. Fenced off as a nature reserve since 1976, it is one of few places in Europe where you can walk the actual site of a meteorite strike, not just read about one.
s: Seven meteorite craters, walkable, on the city's edge
_facts: Located in Morasko, on the northern edge of Poznań
Contains seven meteor craters across 55 hectares
Established as a nature reserve in 1976

w: Despite sitting inside a district confusingly called Nowe Miasto - New Town - this river island is the oldest scrap of Poznan there is: a 10th-century seat of early Polish rulers, before the rest of the city existed. The cathedral and its ecclesiastical buildings still anchor it, listed as a Historic Monument.
s: Called 'New Town', it's actually the oldest part of Poznan
_facts: Island between two branches of the river Warta; name means 'Cathedral Island'
Site of a 10th-century royal palace, making it the oldest part of the city
Poznań Cathedral and other ecclesiastical buildings occupy the island's centre
Designated a Polish national Historic Monument in 2008

w: A neoclassical opera house named for Stanislaw Moniuszko, the composer often called the father of Polish national opera - fitting patronage for a stage that has carried Poznan's opera, operetta and ballet under one grand, colonnaded roof for well over a century.
s: Poznan's opera house, named for the father of Polish opera
_facts: Neoclassical opera house in Poznań
Named after Polish composer Stanisław Moniuszko

w: Poznan's Stary Rynek is the third-largest market square in Poland, ranked only behind Krakow's and Wroclaw's - and it has been the beating heart of the Old Town since the city's medieval founding. Merchant houses, cafes and the town hall with its noontime fighting goats all crowd around its edges.
_facts: Polish name Stary Rynek; centre and oldest part of Poznań's Old Town
Third largest market square in Poland, after Kraków's Main Square and Wrocław's Market Square

w: Two steel crosses - one 19.5 metres, one 21 - lean together on Mickiewicz Square, dated with the years communist Poland's government opened fire on its own workers: 1956, 1968, 1970, 1976, 1980. Unveiled on the 25th anniversary of 1956, they still carry the marchers' slogan: 'For God, for freedom, law, and bread.'
s: Steel crosses dated with every year the state opened fire
_facts: Monument on Adam Mickiewicz Square commemorating the 1956 Poznań protests and later unrest
Unveiled 28 June 1981, the 25th anniversary of the June 1956 events
Two steel crosses, 19.5m and 21m, symbolizing death and resurrection
Carries dates 1956, 1968, 1970, 1976, 1980 and the slogan 'For God, for freedom, law, and bread'

w: A whole museum devoted to a pastry: the Swietomarcinski croissant, a St. Martin's Day tradition 150 years deep in Poznan's baking culture. The visit is interactive - you learn the original recipe hands-on - and it slips in lessons on the local dialect and, naturally, the town hall's fighting goats.
s: A museum built around one very local croissant
_facts: Polish name Rogalowe Muzeum Poznania, at 41 Stary Rynek
Dedicated to the 150-year-old tradition of Świętomarcińskie croissants
Interactive visit teaches the original baking recipe, plus Poznań dialect and town hall goat lore

w: The only freestanding synagogue left standing in Poznan survived the war only because the Wehrmacht wanted a swimming pool: in 1941 the building was gutted and converted into a pool for German soldiers, its interior devastated. It still stands near Rabbi Akiva Eger Square, a scarred but singular survivor.
s: Turned into a Wehrmacht swimming pool in 1941
_facts: Currently the only freestanding synagogue remaining in Poznań
Located at the corner of Wroniecka and Stawna Streets, near Rabbi Akiva Eger Square
Converted into an indoor swimming pool for Wehrmacht soldiers in 1941, devastating the interior
Listed on the Poznań Royal-Imperial Route tourist trail

w: A glass footbridge over the Cybina links a concrete exhibition hall to a restored 19th-century lock, together forming an interactive heritage centre built to explain why the small island across the water mattered so much: Cathedral Island, where the Polish state itself first took shape.
s: A footbridge-museum explaining where Poland began
_facts: Polish name Brama Poznania ICHOT, English name Porta Posnania
Interactive heritage centre dedicated to the history of Cathedral Island (Ostrów Tumski)
Opened 1 May 2014; two buildings linked by a glass footbridge over the Cybina river

w: A public library founded by Count Edward Raczynski, its 1820s facade echoing the Louvre's eastern colonnade - a bit of provincial ambition dressed up as philanthropy. Out front, the goddess Hygieia still pours from a fountain cast by Albert Wolff in 1841, watching over readers heading in to borrow a book.
s: A library with a facade modelled on the Louvre
_facts: Founded by Count Edward Raczyński, building erected 1822-1828
Classical facade features a colonnade reminiscent of the Louvre's eastern facade
Hygieia's Fountain, a statue by Albert Wolff, stands in front, made 1841
